1. Approach and rationale

1.1 Central idea

The supplied evaluator minimizes a nonsmooth, nonconvex finite-dimensional min-max problem:

C5(h) = max_p C_p(h),    C_p(h) = (2/n) sum_i h_i(1-h_{i+d_p}),

where the 2n-1 signed lags are exactly those produced by np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode="full"). There is no useful global convex relaxation because every nonzero-lag term contains the indefinite bilinear product h_i h_{i+d}. The plan therefore does not attempt to solve a convexified surrogate. Instead it repeatedly constructs proposed moves using an exact local directional model of the current maximum set, and accepts a move only when the original, unmodified evaluator strictly improves the accepted candidate. The central primitive is a trust-region linear-programming subproblem that uses the exact gradients of all currently_ACTIVITY_MAX lags to direct the point away from the current maximum ridge while preserving the integral constraint. This is materially different from a smooth epigraph chosen by a simple log-sum-exp descent, a pure cooldown search, or a random-walk strategy: the proposed direction is computed from the exact finite-lag subdifferential of the actual finite-support evaluator.

Subsidiary mechanisms handle stagnation and resolution effects:

- fractional/cyclic coordinate transforms of the parent;
- resolution transfers near the parent length;
- line searches in the tangent directions e_p - e_q, which preserve the sum by construction;
- bounded convex combinations of two feasible candidates, followed by exact re-evaluation;
- deterministic pseudo-random initial starts only when no valid parent exists;
- a final cleanup that rechecks the exact evaluator before returning anything.

The returned number is not a mild relaxation of the original problem. It is always the exact value of the task metric on a vector that has been rechecked for the original discrete feasibility conditions.

A global search in the sphere of feasible approximate neighborhoods or purely random moves can waste effort because the exact max may be controlled by several lag classes. The tangent LP treats those lag classes explicitly. Candidate line searches and blends provide nonlocal escapes from local linearization plateaus, while still accepting only exact-score improvements.

The objective is nonconvex, and local directional methods can only search locally from any assigned seed. No claim of global optimality is made. The LP solution is a local directional proposal, not a certificate of feasibility for a relaxed epigraph. Restraint and nonmonotone line search allow trial proposals but best-candidate bookkeeping is dominated by the exact objective.
